status: COMPLETE — all of §0–§8 + Defaults table + Source ledger captured in lead-1..lead-56 (guide read in full; no content dropped). sections_accounted maps every section to its rules.
note: Faithful rule manifest for generic, repo-agnostic engineering-leadership practice (senior-developer + project-management discipline), distilled from SemVer 2.0.0, Keep a Changelog 1.1.0, Google's eng-practices code-review guides, Conventional Comments, Fowler's Yagni/Technical Debt Quadrant, the Google SRE Book postmortem chapter, Michael Nygard's ADR post, Jeff Bezos's 2016 shareholder letter, and the 2020 Scrum Guide. The .md is authoritative and unchanged; this indexes every actionable rule, typed checkable|judgment|principle, with predicate/reviewer_criterion. §5 (versioning/changelog) covers the ownership/leadership angle only — release-pipeline mechanics belong to the system-operation-maintenance module, not duplicated here.

rules.text: Model engineering leadership as three intertwined disciplines: decompose & scope (turn ambiguous work into small, reviewable, boundable units — §1–§2), verify & respond (code review, risk, incidents — §3–§4, §7), and own the record (versioning, changelog, technical debt, decisions — §5–§6, §8). None of it depends on authority over other people; all of it depends on making the system and the team's shared understanding of it legible.

Two axes recur throughout: reversibility — can this be cheaply undone, and therefore made fast and delegated, or is it a one-way door that deserves slower deliberation (§4)? — and legibility — will someone who wasn't in the room be able to reconstruct why this was done from what got written down (a PR description, a changelog entry, a postmortem, an ADR — §3, §5, §7–§8)?

'Better, not perfect' is the load-bearing standard threaded through code review (§3), scope control (§2), and technical-debt tradeoffs (§6) alike. Google's own code-review documentation: 'there is no such thing as perfect code—there is only better code. Reviewers should not require the author to polish every tiny piece of a CL before granting approval.' The goal everywhere below is a codebase/system/team that is measurably improving over time, in small reviewable increments. [VERIFIED, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/standard.html]

Decompose work into units that are independently reviewable and independently revertible — the same logic that governs code review governs task breakdown. A unit should be small enough that one reviewer can hold its entire diff in their head, and rejecting/rolling it back doesn't take unrelated work down with it. [VERIFIED, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/small-cls.html]

predicate.spec: each planned unit of work has a diff/scope small enough for a single reviewer to fully hold, and can be rejected or reverted without pulling in unrelated work.

rules.text: When work seems to require one large, indivisible change, treat that as a signal to look harder for a decomposition (e.g. a refactor-first unit) before accepting the large unit as necessary — genuinely needing an unsplittable large CL is 'very rarely' true. [VERIFIED, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/small-cls.html — Can't Make it Small Enough]

predicate.spec: before starting a large/indivisible unit of work, a decomposition attempt (e.g. refactor-first split, teammate consultation) is documented as having been tried.

rules.text: Prefer stacking small increments (send one small unit for review, immediately start the next based on it) over batching all work into one large handoff — keeps reviewers unblocked, avoids wasted work if an early direction is rejected, avoids blocking on review. [VERIFIED, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/small-cls.html]
rules.reviewer_criterion: Is work being planned/sent as a sequence of small, independently reviewable increments (stacked or otherwise), rather than one large batched handoff?

rules.text: Treat every estimate as a range with a confidence level, not a single point number, and re-estimate openly when new information changes the shape of the work rather than defending the original guess. [INFERRED — standard practitioner convention, no primary source fetched.]
rules.reviewer_criterion: Was the estimate communicated as a range/confidence rather than a bare point number, and was it revisited when the shape of the work materially changed?

rules.text: For novel or uncertain work, prefer sizing relative to a known reference unit ('about as involved as X') over an absolute hours/days figure — relative sizing is easier to calibrate than absolute estimates, which compound error under uncertainty. [INFERRED — standard practitioner convention, no primary source fetched.]
rules.reviewer_criterion: For uncertain work, is the size expressed relative to a known comparable unit rather than as an unqualified absolute-time figure?

rules.text: Work from an explicit, WRITTEN Definition of Done as the quality bar for every unit of work: 'The Definition of Done is a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product... If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented.' Work is done when it meets the agreed, written bar — not when it compiles or feels finished. [VERIFIED, scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html]

predicate.spec: a written Definition of Done exists and is checked before any unit of work is considered releasable/presentable; an item failing it returns to the backlog rather than shipping.

rules.text: Treat adherence to the Definition of Done as a standing accountability of whoever is doing the work, not a gate imposed afterward by someone else — the Scrum Guide lists 'instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done' as a core accountability alongside planning and adapting. [VERIFIED, scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html — Developers]

predicate.spec: the people doing the work self-check against the Definition of Done as they go, not only a separate gatekeeper after the fact.

rules.text: YAGNI — do not build a capability merely because you presume the software will need it in the future. Build the problem known to need solving now; the future problem, once it actually arrives, can be solved with its real, observed shape, which speculative up-front design cannot correctly anticipate. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/Yagni.html]

predicate.spec: no capability is added to satisfy a presumed/speculative future need that is not backed by a concrete, present requirement.

rules.text: Treat over-engineering (code made more generic than needed, or functionality added that isn't presently needed) as a defect a reviewer should flag, same as any other complexity problem — 'solve the problem they know needs to be solved now, not the problem that the developer speculates might need to be solved in the future.' [VERIFIED, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/looking-for.html — Complexity]

predicate.spec: code review explicitly checks for and flags over-engineering / speculative generality as a complexity issue, not only functional correctness.

rules.text: Apply scope control per-decision, not as a blanket refusal to ever design for extension — YAGNI does not mean 'never generalize'; the burden of proof sits with the speculative feature, and the default without that proof is 'not yet.' [INFERRED — synthesis of lead-11 and lead-12; no single primary source states this framing verbatim.]
rules.reviewer_criterion: For any generalization or 'just in case' capability, has its need been demonstrated by a concrete, present requirement — rather than assumed for a hypothetical future one?

rules.text: Write acceptance criteria before implementation begins, as concrete, testable, falsifiable statements — a criterion nothing could fail to satisfy is not a criterion. This turns a Definition of Done (lead-9) from a general quality bar into a specific, checkable bar for one piece of work. [INFERRED — standard BDD/agile convention, no primary source fetched.]
rules.reviewer_criterion: Do the acceptance criteria for this unit of work exist before the implementation, and is each one concrete enough that a reviewer could point to evidence proving it was or wasn't met?

rules.text: Default to small CLs/PRs: 'the right size for a CL is one self-contained change' that 'makes a minimal change that addresses just one thing,' includes its own related test code, and errs toward too-small over too-large. Small changes are reviewed more quickly/thoroughly, less likely to hide a bug, waste less work if rejected, easier to merge, simpler to roll back cleanly. [VERIFIED, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/small-cls.html]

predicate.spec: each CL/PR addresses one self-contained change, includes its own related tests, and errs toward smaller rather than larger scope.

rules.text: When a change genuinely cannot be made small, treat it as a documented exception path, not silent noncompliance: get the reviewer's advance consent, warn them what's coming, be extra diligent about tests. [VERIFIED, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/small-cls.html — Can't Make it Small Enough]

predicate.spec: a large/unsplittable CL only proceeds after explicit advance reviewer consent and with heightened test diligence, not silently.

rules.text: As reviewer, favor approving a CL once it definitely improves the overall code health of the system, even if it isn't perfect — 'there is no such thing as perfect code—there is only better code. Reviewers should not require the author to polish every tiny piece of a CL before granting approval.' Balance protecting code health against developers' need to make forward progress. [VERIFIED verbatim, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/standard.html]

predicate.spec: approval is granted once a CL definitely improves overall code health, without requiring every minor/polish-level point to be resolved first.

rules.text: Run a fixed rubric on every review: design, functionality (incl. UI and parallel/concurrent code), complexity (incl. over-engineering), tests (present and well-designed), naming, comments (why not what), documentation, and house-style conformance. [VERIFIED, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/looking-for.html — Summary]

predicate.spec: the review checklist covers design, functionality, complexity, tests, naming, comments, documentation, and style — not an ad hoc subset.

rules.text: Review every line assigned and understand what it does — don't skim and assume; if code is too hard to follow, ask the author to clarify rather than approving blind. Also look at the CL in its wider file/system context, and never accept a CL that degrades the code health of the system even by a small amount — most systems become complex through accumulated small, individually-accepted complexities. [VERIFIED, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/looking-for.html — Every Line, Context]

predicate.spec: every assigned line is read and understood (clarification requested if not), the surrounding file/system context is checked, and CLs that would degrade overall code health are not approved.

rules.text: Label the severity of review comments so the author can triage correctly: 'Nit:' (minor, technically correct, low-impact), 'Optional'/'Consider:' (good idea, not required), 'FYI:' (not expected in this change). Unlabeled comments default to being read as mandatory. [VERIFIED, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/comments.html — Label comment severity]

predicate.spec: non-mandatory review comments are explicitly labeled by severity (e.g. Nit/Optional/FYI or equivalent), distinguishing required changes from suggestions from pure information.

rules.text: Structure each comment as label [+ optional decoration]: subject, with reasoning/next-steps in the body — e.g. 'suggestion (non-blocking): rename this for clarity.' Recommended labels: praise, nitpick, suggestion, issue, todo, question, thought; recommended decorations: (blocking), (non-blocking), (if-minor). [VERIFIED, conventionalcomments.org — Format, Labels, Decorations]

predicate.spec: review comments follow a label[+decoration]: subject [discussion] format using a defined label/decoration vocabulary, rather than free-form unlabeled prose.

rules.text: Comment on the code, never the developer, especially when contentious — Google's example: bad 'Why did you use threads here...'; good 'The concurrency model here is adding complexity... without any actual performance benefit.' Explain reasoning rather than issuing a bare verdict; balance explicit direction against naming the problem and letting the developer choose the fix. [VERIFIED, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/comments.html — Courtesy, Summary]

predicate.spec: review comments critique the code/design, never the developer as a person, and include the reasoning behind a requested change rather than a bare directive.

rules.text: Actively look for something to sincerely praise in every review, and never leave false praise — false praise is actively damaging, not neutral. [VERIFIED, conventionalcomments.org — Labels, praise row]

predicate.spec: each review includes at least an attempt to find a genuine, specific positive to call out, and no praise comment is left insincerely.

rules.text: Respond to a review request within one business day at the latest, even if the full in-depth review must follow later — silence, not a review taking a few rounds, is what blocks a team. [VERIFIED, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/speed.html]

predicate.spec: first response to a review request occurs within one business day of the request.

rules.text: When author and reviewer cannot reach consensus through comments, escalate deliberately: try a synchronous conversation, record its outcome back on the CL, then follow a defined escalation path (broader team discussion, tech lead, code maintainer, or eng manager). 'Don't let a CL sit around because the author and the reviewer can't come to an agreement.' [VERIFIED verbatim, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/standard.html — Resolving Conflicts]

predicate.spec: an unresolved review disagreement proceeds through consensus attempt → recorded synchronous discussion → a named escalation path, and is never simply left unresolved indefinitely.

rules.text: Sort every non-trivial decision by reversibility first and let that dictate process weight: 'Many decisions are reversible, two-way doors. Those decisions can use a light-weight process.' A cheaply reversible decision should be made fast, lightweight, often delegated; applying a heavyweight process uniformly is itself a cost. [VERIFIED, aboutamazon.com/news/company-news/2016-letter-to-shareholders — High-Velocity Decision Making]

predicate.spec: decisions are explicitly classified by reversibility, and reversible ('two-way door') decisions use a lighter-weight, faster, more delegated process than irreversible ones.

rules.text: For a reversible decision, don't wait for near-certainty: 'most decisions should probably be made with somewhere around 70% of the information you wish you had. If you wait for 90%, in most cases, you're probably being slow.' Pair with being good at quickly recognizing and correcting a wrong decision. [VERIFIED, aboutamazon.com/news/company-news/2016-letter-to-shareholders]

predicate.spec: reversible decisions are made at roughly ~70% of desired information rather than waiting for ~90%+, paired with a mechanism to detect and correct a wrong call quickly.

rules.text: When you have conviction on a direction but no consensus, say so explicitly and ask collaborators to 'disagree and commit' rather than silently overriding them or letting disagreement stall the decision. Reserve this for decisions reversible enough to gamble on; use slower consensus-seeking process for irreversible/safety-critical calls. [VERIFIED, aboutamazon.com/news/company-news/2016-letter-to-shareholders]
rules.reviewer_criterion: Was 'disagree and commit' invoked only to unblock a reversible decision under genuine disagreement (not to silence dissent, and not on an irreversible/safety-critical call)?

rules.text: Rank identified risks by likelihood × impact, then apply reversibility as a third multiplier: a low-likelihood, high-impact, irreversible risk should outrank a higher-likelihood but cheaply-reversible one, even if a naive likelihood×impact score alone wouldn't show it. [INFERRED — standard risk-management practice combined with lead-26's reversibility axis; no single primary source fetched for this three-factor framing.]
rules.reviewer_criterion: Does the risk ranking explicitly account for reversibility, not just likelihood and impact — i.e. would a low-likelihood but irreversible risk be caught even if its naive score looks small?

rules.text: Escalate a stuck decision or unresolved risk rather than letting it sit unaddressed — the same discipline as code-review conflict resolution (lead-25) generalizes to any stalled call: attempt consensus, hold a recorded synchronous conversation if needed, then follow a defined escalation path. Don't let indecision itself become the risk. [VERIFIED, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/standard.html — Resolving Conflicts, applied here to the general risk/decision case]

predicate.spec: a stalled decision or unaddressed risk is escalated via a defined path (consensus attempt → recorded discussion → named escalation route) rather than left indefinitely unresolved.

rules.text: Declare a public API explicitly (in code or documentation) before making any SemVer compatibility promise about it — SemVer's contract only covers what has been declared public. [VERIFIED, semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html, item 1]

predicate.spec: a public API is explicitly declared (in code or docs) before SemVer compatibility guarantees are made about it.

rules.text: Own the version-number triple: increment MAJOR for incompatible API changes, MINOR for backward-compatible new functionality (also required on any deprecation), PATCH for backward-compatible bug fixes only; reset MINOR/PATCH to 0 on a MAJOR bump, PATCH to 0 on a MINOR bump. [VERIFIED, semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html — Summary and items 6-8]

predicate.spec: version bumps follow MAJOR=incompatible/MINOR=compatible-feature-or-deprecation/PATCH=compatible-bugfix-only, with lower components reset to 0 on a higher-component bump.

rules.text: Treat a MAJOR bump as a deliberate cost/benefit decision, not a number to avoid incrementing: 'Having to bump major versions to release incompatible changes means you'll think through the impact of your changes, and evaluate the cost/benefit ratio involved.' [VERIFIED, semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html — FAQ]
rules.reviewer_criterion: Was a backward-incompatible change actually shipped as a MAJOR bump (rather than disguised as MINOR/PATCH to avoid a 'big number'), with the cost/benefit of the break considered first?

rules.text: Once a version is published, its contents are immutable — any correction ships as a new version number; a released version is never silently edited in place. [VERIFIED, semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html, item 3]

predicate.spec: no published version's contents are modified after release; any fix, however small, is released under a new version number.

rules.text: Own the decision of when to leave 0.y.z 'initial development' (anything MAY change, API not stable) and commit to 1.0.0: do it once the software is in production, has an API users depend on, or you find yourself worrying about breaking it. Staying below 1.0.0 indefinitely is itself a decision telling consumers 'nothing here is stable yet.' [VERIFIED, semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html, item 4 and FAQ]

predicate.spec: the project explicitly decides and documents when to move from 0.y.z to 1.0.0, based on production use / a depended-upon API / active concern about breaking it — not left as an unexamined default.

rules.text: Own the changelog as a document for humans, not a git-log dump — group entries under Added/Changed/Deprecated/Removed/Fixed/Security, list latest version first, date every release, state whether SemVer is followed. [VERIFIED, keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/ — tagline, Guiding Principles, Types of changes]

predicate.spec: the changelog groups entries under the six Keep a Changelog types, orders the latest version first, dates every release, and states its SemVer adherence.

rules.text: Maintain a live 'Unreleased' section at the top of the changelog so upcoming changes are visible before they ship; move its contents under the new version heading at release time. [VERIFIED, keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/ — How can I reduce the effort required to maintain a changelog?]

predicate.spec: an Unreleased section exists at the top of the changelog and its entries are moved under a dated version heading at each release.

rules.text: Write each changelog entry for the consumer deciding whether to upgrade, not for yourself remembering what you did — state the user-visible effect, not the internal diff; a changelog and a commit log serve different readers. [VERIFIED, keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/ — tagline and Guiding Principles]
rules.reviewer_criterion: Does the changelog entry describe the user-visible effect of the change (what a consumer needs to know before upgrading), rather than restating the commit/diff itself?

rules.text: Reserve the technical-debt metaphor for a considered, short-term-beneficial decision to adopt an unsustainable design strategy (e.g. to make a release) — not for 'a mess,' code merely poorly made by people unaware of better practice. Conflating the two blunts the metaphor's value for communicating a real tradeoff to non-technical stakeholders. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/TechnicalDebtQuadrant.html, citing Robert C. Martin's 'a mess is not a technical debt']

predicate.spec: the term 'technical debt' is applied only to considered, tradeoff-driven design decisions, not used interchangeably with ordinary poor-quality/messy code.

rules.text: Classify debt on two independent axes — reckless vs. prudent (was the tradeoff a considered, informed choice?) and deliberate vs. inadvertent (taken on knowingly, or only visible in hindsight?) — because the appropriate response differs by quadrant: prudent-deliberate debt is a legitimate, trackable tradeoff; reckless-deliberate debt (choosing 'quick and dirty' believing clean code can't be afforded) is close to negligence. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/TechnicalDebtQuadrant.html]

predicate.spec: tracked debt items are classified along both the reckless/prudent axis and the deliberate/inadvertent axis, and the response (accept/track vs. treat as a process failure) differs by quadrant.

rules.text: Expect prudent-inadvertent debt as a normal cost of learning while building — it is common for a team to realize partway through a project what the design should have been from the start; this kind of debt 'is inevitable and thus should be expected,' even from the best teams, and is not evidence of a mistake to assign blame for. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/TechnicalDebtQuadrant.html]

predicate.spec: debt discovered in hindsight from legitimate design learning (prudent-inadvertent) is tracked as expected/normal, not treated as a blame-worthy error.

rules.text: For any debt knowingly carried, decide explicitly whether you are paying ongoing interest or scheduling a payoff of the principal — an unpaid debt keeps costing (interest); refactoring toward the better design pays down the principal. A prudent debt with small interest payments may legitimately not be worth paying down — but that call should be explicit, not default. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/TechnicalDebtQuadrant.html]

predicate.spec: each tracked debt item has an explicit interest-vs-principal disposition recorded (accept ongoing cost vs. scheduled payoff), not left undecided by default.

rules.text: Never pay down debt, or hit a deadline, by weakening the gate that measures code health — a lint rule, a test, a coverage threshold, an acceptance criterion. That converts visible, trackable debt into invisible risk, the opposite of what the debt metaphor is for. [INFERRED — direct extension of lead-39–lead-42's debt-tracking discipline; no primary source states this specific anti-pattern verbatim.]

predicate.spec: no lint rule, test, coverage threshold, or acceptance criterion is loosened as a means of resolving technical debt or meeting a deadline; the underlying condition is fixed instead.

rules.text: Define incident/postmortem triggers before an incident happens, not during one: user-visible downtime/degradation past a threshold, any data loss, on-call engineer intervention (rollback, rerouting), resolution time above a threshold, or a monitoring failure meaning the incident was found manually. Pre-defining the bar avoids mid-incident argument about whether 'this counts.' [VERIFIED, sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/ — Google's Postmortem Philosophy]

predicate.spec: postmortem/incident-review trigger criteria are documented in advance (downtime/degradation, data loss, on-call intervention, resolution-time threshold, monitoring-failure discovery), not decided ad hoc during an incident.

rules.text: Write every qualifying incident up with the goal of documentation, root-cause understanding, and concrete preventive action — never as punishment: 'Writing a postmortem is not punishment—it is a learning opportunity for the entire company.' [VERIFIED verbatim, sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/]

predicate.spec: every incident meeting the defined triggers produces a write-up covering documentation, root cause(s), and concrete preventive follow-up actions.

rules.text: Keep the retro blameless — critique the actions and system that allowed the incident, never the person: 'Removing blame from a postmortem gives people the confidence to escalate issues without fear.' A blame culture teaches people to hide incidents rather than surface them. [VERIFIED verbatim, sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/]

predicate.spec: postmortem write-ups and discussions critique actions/systems, never name-and-blame an individual; no punitive consequence is attached to being named in a postmortem.

rules.text: Do not stigmatize a person or team that produces incident write-ups often — punishing that visibility 'risks creating a culture in which incidents and issues are swept under the rug,' raising organizational risk rather than lowering it. [VERIFIED, sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/]

predicate.spec: frequency of postmortems authored by a person/team is not used as a negative signal against them (e.g. in review, standing, or workload decisions).

rules.text: During an active incident, separate 'make it stop' from 'understand why': mitigate first (rollback, reroute, fail over), defer full root-cause analysis to the calm, blameless postmortem process afterward rather than attempting deep RCA while the system is still degraded. [INFERRED — standard incident-response practice, consistent with but not verbatim from the SRE trigger material cited in lead-44.]
rules.reviewer_criterion: During the incident itself, was effort spent on mitigation/rollback first, with deep root-cause analysis explicitly deferred to the postmortem rather than attempted mid-incident?

rules.text: Communicate incident status in plain, factual, blame-free language while it's ongoing — what's affected, what's being done, what isn't yet known. The same code-not-person discipline from review (lead-22) and the blameless retro (lead-46) applies to real-time incident communication. [INFERRED — synthesis of lead-22 and lead-46; no single primary source fetched for real-time incident communication wording.]
rules.reviewer_criterion: Was incident status communicated in plain, factual terms (impact, current action, known unknowns) without assigning blame to an individual, while the incident was still active?

rules.text: Write an Architecture Decision Record for every 'architecturally significant' decision — one affecting structure, non-functional characteristics, dependencies, interfaces, or construction techniques. Keep ADRs as short text files in a lightweight markup (Markdown/Textile), in the project repository, numbered sequentially and monotonically with numbers never reused. [VERIFIED, cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions]

predicate.spec: architecturally-significant decisions (structure/non-functional/dependency/interface/construction-technique) each produce a short, repo-tracked, sequentially-numbered ADR file in a lightweight markup format.

rules.text: Structure each ADR with five parts, one or two pages total: Title (short noun phrase); Context (forces at play — technological/political/social/project-local, value-neutral); Decision (the response, full sentences, active voice, e.g. 'We will...'); Status (proposed/accepted/deprecated/superseded-with-reference); Consequences (all resulting effects — positive, negative, neutral). [VERIFIED, cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions]

predicate.spec: each ADR contains Title, Context, Decision, Status, and Consequences sections, with Consequences listing effects beyond only the favorable ones, and stays roughly one to two pages.

rules.text: When a decision is reversed, keep the old ADR and mark it superseded rather than deleting or silently editing it — 'It's still relevant to know that it was the decision, but is no longer the decision.' Same supersede-don't-delete discipline as any durable, audited record. [VERIFIED, cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions]

predicate.spec: a reversed decision's original ADR is retained and marked superseded (with a reference to the replacement), never deleted or rewritten in place.

rules.text: Write the ADR's Context so a future team member who wasn't in the room has a real third option beyond blindly accepting a decision (fine if still valid, corrosive if the context changed unnoticed) or blindly changing it (fine if it needed reversing, dangerous if it silently reintroduces the original problem). A recorded rationale is what makes 'understand, then decide' possible. [VERIFIED, cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions — Context]

predicate.spec: the Context section records enough of the original forces/rationale that a newcomer can decide whether the decision still holds, rather than only being able to blindly accept or blindly overturn it.

rules.text: In review comments, ADRs, and postmortems alike, write to explain why, not restate what — 'comments are useful when they explain why some code exists, and should not be explaining what some code is doing... if the code isn't clear enough to explain itself, the code should be made simpler.' This is exactly the reasoning an ADR's Context exists to capture (lead-53). [VERIFIED, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/looking-for.html — Comments]

predicate.spec: comments/ADR-context/postmortem prose explain the reasoning behind a choice (why), rather than restating what is already visible in the code/config/timeline itself.

rules.text: Treat every review comment and piece of feedback as a teaching opportunity, not only a gate: 'Code review can have an important function of teaching developers... if your comment is purely educational, but not critical..., prefix it with Nit: or otherwise indicate that it's not mandatory.' Balance giving an explicit instruction against naming the problem and letting the engineer reach the fix themselves. [VERIFIED, google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/standard.html — Mentoring, and .../reviewer/comments.html — Summary]
rules.reviewer_criterion: Is purely educational feedback clearly marked as non-mandatory (e.g. 'Nit:'), and does at least some feedback point out the problem and let the author choose the fix, rather than dictating every fix explicitly?

rules.text: Write for the reader with the LEAST context, not the one with the most — a decision record, postmortem, or review comment that only makes sense to someone already in the conversation has failed at the one thing it exists to do. [INFERRED — synthesis of lead-53's ADR rationale and the Scrum Guide's 'shared understanding' framing of the Definition of Done; no single primary source fetched for this framing.]
rules.reviewer_criterion: Could someone with no prior context on this decision/incident/change understand it from the written record alone, without needing to ask the author for missing background?

sections_accounted.§0 executive summary — the practices, th: lead-1 (three intertwined disciplines), lead-2 (reversibility + legibility axes), lead-3 (better-not-perfect standard, verbatim Google quote)
